main_message: Gibraltar was fought over for centuries because of its position at the Strait, and the old fight over the Rock has become a modern argument over the border, jobs and sovereignty.

claims_doubted.quote: Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
claims_doubted.why: Counts vary a lot. Sayer's 'fourteen' is a Victorian British tally. Spanish authors list different numbers, and they disagree on which blockades and attacks count as sieges. 'Both sides agree' is too strong. Also, the title says 'besieged 14 times' but the video never lists them. It only covers 1704, 1727 and 1779-83, so the title promise is not kept.

claims_doubted.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
claims_doubted.why: Too short. It leaves out that the Spanish crown went to Philip V by Charles II's will, and that the war was about the whole European balance. In 1704 the Spanish garrison was also loyal to Philip V, which is why the Spanish side calls it a conquest by a foreign fleet. The video does not say that.

claims_doubted.quote: Britain said in 2015 that it does.
claims_doubted.why: Vague and no source on screen. This is the most disputed point in the whole story (the isthmus), and it gets one flat sentence with nothing to check. The British position is also older than 2015. Spain's argument rests on the treaty text and on the legal principle that land not ceded is not British.

The 1704-05 siege is described as 'with French troops' but not how close it came, and the 1727 siege is skipped over. These two sieges are the ones that explain why the 1730 line was built, so the explanation is thin.

claims_doubted.quote: Based at Algeciras, its boats were there to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
claims_doubted.why: Fine as far as it goes, but the video does not say that Spain's use of Algeciras was only possible because the city had been refounded in the 1700s by people who left Gibraltar. As an Algeciras person I would want that connection. Also 'its boats' were gunboats (jabeques), and the Spanish blockade was often broken by Barceló's own difficulties and by the weather, which the video does not mention.

claims_doubted.quote: By the next afternoon, all ten batteries were lost.
claims_doubted.why: Simplified. Several batteries were burned by red-hot shot during the night, and the Spanish and French commanders also had to burn some of their own to stop capture. Calling it 'lost' hides who destroyed them.

claims_doubted.quote: The blockade never forced a surrender.
claims_doubted.why: True, but it omits that the garrison was close to running out of food several times, and that the 1783 peace was decided in Paris and Versailles, not on the Rock. Also Gibraltar was kept by Britain in the 1783 Treaty of Versailles. The video says 'Gibraltar stayed British' in a way that reads as a military result when it was a diplomatic one (Spain got Menorca and Florida back instead).

claims_doubted.quote: With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
claims_doubted.why: The source says 'with Spanish authorisation', but the video makes it sound like routine cooperation. The forts around San Roque and the line were destroyed to keep them from the French. The date is also given as 1810 on screen with a note that Montero says 1811. This is the right way to flag a discrepancy, but the narration chooses one date silently.

claims_doubted.quote: Behind the fence: a garrison camp, gardens, rifle ranges, a racecourse.
claims_doubted.why: No source. The reader thinks these were all built on the neutral ground, and the video never says that they were put there by Britain without Spanish agreement. It is stated as a neutral description of a list.

claims_doubted.quote: Gibraltar counts about fifty-five kilometres of tunnels from every era, more than its roads above ground.
claims_doubted.why: A frequently repeated figure without a clear source. 'More than its roads above ground' is a tourist-guide line and should be checked before being stated as fact.

claims_doubted.quote: By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.
claims_doubted.why: Operation Torch was commanded from Gibraltar (Eisenhower's HQ in the tunnels), true, but 'run from inside the Rock' is an overstatement for the whole invasion, which had a much wider command structure. Also the video skips Spain's wartime role: Franco's Spain allowed German agents to watch the Strait and the Gibraltar harbour.

claims_doubted.quote: no complaint over the airstrip is on record.
claims_doubted.why: This is a heavy claim built on one scholar's statement and presented in a silent-shot context, so it lands as 'Spain accepted it'. Spain protested in 1939 and the Spanish position has always been that the isthmus was occupied illegally. The video gives the 1939 protest, but then puts the 'no record' line right after, which weakens the Spanish claim by implication.

claims_doubted.quote: Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off.
claims_doubted.why: Source is British, which the video says. But it leaves out why Spain closed the frontier in 1969 (the Gibraltar Constitution Order, which gave Gibraltarians a larger say over their own government and which Spain saw as against UN decolonisation resolutions), and that Franco's Spain was then a dictatorship. Also it says nothing about the 1967 referendum or the UN resolutions.

Pedestrian access was partly opened in 1982 and the full opening was in February 1985. It is correct but it misses that the opening was tied to the Brussels Agreement of 1984 and the Lisbon Agreement to talk about sovereignty. A quick fact, but it leaves out a political step.

claims_doubted.quote: Our read: part of the work behind that number is done from the other side.
claims_doubted.why: An opinion in the middle of the data. It is flagged as 'our read', which is honest, but the video then draws a conclusion for the viewer. Per-resident output is also not unusual for places with many cross-border workers (Luxembourg, Monaco), and the video does not give that context. It also ignores that Gibraltar's output depends on its tax and financial system, which is exactly what Spain complains about.

one_sided.quote: Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
one_sided.why: Opens with the British-Gibraltar view of the present as the normal state. Spanish residents of the Campo de Gibraltar would frame it as the end of decades of difficult crossings at the fence, but also the treaty is still provisional, which the video says only at the end.

one_sided.quote: Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender.
one_sided.why: This is a fair point for Spain, and I like that it names the source. But the next sentences give the British count of 'up to five hundred', so the video is balanced here. I would only say the phrase 'the fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds' has no counter and no source at all.

one_sided.quote: Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third."
one_sided.why: Makes the terms sound generous. From the Spanish side the people who left did so because they would not accept a foreign flag, and many of them took the sacred images and the town's records with them and founded San Roque. The video mentions San Roque but not that the exiles still consider San Roque the true Gibraltar ('the City of Gibraltar in exile'), and that matters to Spanish memory.

one_sided.quote: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever."
one_sided.why: Quotes the 'for ever' of Article X, but the same article also includes the clause that if Britain ever gives up the Rock, Spain gets first refusal. The video quotes the 'without territorial jurisdiction' limit, which is good, but it leaves out the first-refusal clause, which is the basis of Spain's present claim. It is the most important Spanish legal point in the treaty.

one_sided.quote: Based at Algeciras, its boats were there to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
one_sided.why: The whole Great Siege chapter is told mostly through the garrison's suffering (thistles, scurvy, eggs at sixpence). The Spanish side has no equivalent human detail. We hear nothing about Spanish troops, the siege camps, disease in the Spanish lines or the people of the Campo.

one_sided.quote: Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
one_sided.why: Only a British officer's excuse is given. The civilians who 'fled south' and the town being bombarded are mentioned briefly, but the video does not say the bombardment destroyed most of the town. The reader gets the soldiers' looting softened by an officer's explanation.

one_sided.quote: The garrison turned to heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire.
one_sided.why: Told as clever tactics, with a heroic tone. The victims (the sailors and soldiers burning in the batteries) are told later only as numbers. The 'Their answer to red-hot shot' line frames Spain and France as the ones who had to answer, which makes Britain the active side.

Placing '16 killed' next to '> 2,000 lost' for the same day is a very strong contrast and the viewer will take it as a British win. The numbers are probably right, but there is no mention that the Spanish and French also pulled many men out of the burning batteries (the figure of 357 rescued is British credit; the video does not say that Spanish and French boats rescued others).

one_sided.quote: The Duc de Crillon led the siege.
one_sided.why: A small thing: Crillon was French in Spanish service. The video does not explain that, and Spanish readers would also expect the name of the Spanish naval commander, Admiral Luis de Córdova, and the Spanish gunboat commander Antonio Barceló, who are missing completely.

one_sided.quote: June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier.
one_sided.why: Brings in Spain's pro-Axis behaviour as a one-line fact in the middle of the runway story. It is true, but it is not balanced by the British side of the same moment (for example that Britain used the airfield and the evacuation of civilians to a country that was officially neutral, and the later sealing of Spanish workers' access).

one_sided.quote: For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested what it called breaches of Spanish waters; no complaint over the airstrip is on record.
one_sided.why: The video uses a Spanish scholar to say Spain did not complain, which is a strong support for the British position that the airfield was tolerated. A neutral telling would add that Spain was in a very weak position during the war and that the later UN-era protests were constant.

one_sided.quote: Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
one_sided.why: Takes the Gibraltar government's figure as the headline, then comments on it. La Línea's unemployment is given too, so there is some balance, but the video lets the viewer see the contrast and does not explain Spanish concerns on tax, smuggling, or the effect on the Campo.

one_sided.quote: In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty; the next day, routine checks here ended.
one_sided.why: Presents the treaty as UK-EU only and does not say what the Spanish government's role was, or what the treaty means for the Spanish and Gibraltar positions on sovereignty. A short line says it 'changes neither side's position', but it does not say Spain's view in Spain's words.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
casualty_counter_missing.why: In 1704, no source for the number of rounds. It sits right after a Spanish count of the garrison, so the viewer will assume it is the same Spanish source, but it is not stated.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By October, by the British count, about fourteen thousand Spanish troops faced the Rock.
casualty_counter_missing.why: This one does name the counter. Fine. I mention it because it contrasts with the places where the counter is missing.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By British tallies, the two sides fired over four hundred and sixty thousand rounds.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Says 'British tallies' but not which tally or who in Britain counted it. Fourteen thousand and four hundred and sixty thousand rounds are not neutral numbers and the Spanish count is not given.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By September 1782, the garrison counted about seven and a half thousand men.
casualty_counter_missing.why: OK for the garrison, but there is no Spanish or French number for the besiegers' strength at the same date, so the reader cannot compare.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By British and Spanish counts, over two thousand attackers were lost, prisoners included; the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
casualty_counter_missing.why: 'British and Spanish counts' is two sources merged into one number, and the on-screen card says 'British estimate & Montero'. Montero is a Spanish historian writing in 1860, not a count made at the time. The French account from 1785 says 185 hit by gunfire, which is far lower, and the narration does not explain the big gap between 185 and 2,000+. A viewer will not know which to believe.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: From all causes, the Spanish historian Montero put the losses near two thousand defenders and six thousand besiegers.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Names Montero, which is good, but his 2,000 for the defenders conflicts with the garrison's own 869, and the video puts the two side by side without telling the viewer that Montero is a secondary source writing 80 years later, while the garrison return is a primary record. The reader gets two numbers and no guidance.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Source named as 'Britain' (government). The Spanish count of workers affected, which would include families and the Campo economy, is missing.

hard_to_follow.quote: In 1782, ten floating batteries came to break it.
hard_to_follow.why: A listener has no idea what a floating battery is, and the hook jumps from 1782 to 1941 to the present in three lines. It is a teaser, but heard once it is confusing.

hard_to_follow.quote: Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of the rival claimant, "Charles the Third."
hard_to_follow.why: Two Georges, an admiral and a prince, and a 'Charles the Third' who is not the Charles III of 1779 that appears later. Heard once, it is a mess of names. 'Charles the Third' for the Habsburg claimant and 'Charles III' for the Bourbon king of Spain in 1779 will confuse the listener.

hard_to_follow.quote: On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered.
hard_to_follow.why: The date on screen (4 Aug vs 24 July old calendar) is only on screen. If you only listen, the dates 24 July and 4 August seem to disagree and nobody explains Julian and Gregorian.

hard_to_follow.quote: But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
hard_to_follow.why: A long legal quote that is spoken fast. A listener will not understand what it means in practice.

hard_to_follow.quote: Spain besieged it twice more: from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and in 1727.
hard_to_follow.why: Dates stacked in one sentence. 'Twice more' after 1704 and then '1704 to 1705' sounds like a counting error.

hard_to_follow.quote: Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets gathered in the bay: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
hard_to_follow.why: Numbers, two counters, and 'ships of the line' all at once. Heard once, only 'about fifty' sticks.

hard_to_follow.quote: The thirteenth of September 1782. That morning, the batteries moved into position, and the garrison opened fire on them. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, the attackers' guns, some four hundred, opened fire together.
hard_to_follow.why: The most important day, but the order is confusing: the garrison fires first, then the attackers fire at 10:25. Hard to picture who did what.
Four numbers on one card (2,000, 185, 357, 16) while the narrator reads a long sentence. Too much to take in at once.

hard_to_follow.quote: By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
hard_to_follow.why: Arrives after the battle chapter but it is set 'before the attack', so the timeline goes backwards. A listener is lost for a moment.

hard_to_follow.quote: Remember this street in La Línea. We'll come back to it.
hard_to_follow.why: Only makes sense with the picture. For an audio-only listener, nothing tells which street.

hard_to_follow.quote: That spreads output over the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs.
hard_to_follow.why: Dense economics. Output per resident, residents vs workers, and two different numbers (14,000 jobs and 15,000 crossers) in the same chapter. Heard once, nobody can follow it.

hard_to_follow.quote: As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is applied provisionally, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
hard_to_follow.why: Stacks a date, a legal term and a future event. 'Applied provisionally' is a technical phrase that most viewers will not understand.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many
boring_or_slow.why: This chapter is the longest one and is mostly a chain of dates, counts and small events (relief fleets, stores, scurvy, rounds fired, garrison numbers). The human part is good, but between the starvation and the 13 September battle there is a long list of facts with no story pull.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: Before the attack, all summer, the garrison had been digging through the north face.
boring_or_slow.why: A tunnelling digression right in the middle of the climax. The viewer wants to know what happened on 13 September, and gets rock-cutting figures instead.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.
boring_or_slow.why: A hundred years are covered in a few lines with no event, no person, no map change you can follow. This is where a viewer would drift.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: Inside the Rock, those tunnels held a road about a mile long, a hospital and a power station
boring_or_slow.why: A tourist-style tunnel tour that does not move the argument forward, followed by a silent shot, then a numbers line (650 aircraft). The thread about sovereignty is lost for a minute.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident
boring_or_slow.why: A string of statistics (jobs share, crossers, unemployment rank, output per head) with little story. The ending recap is better than this middle.

top3_fixes: Keep the promise of the title or change the title: either list all fourteen sieges in a quick animated timeline (1309 to 1783) with who attacked and who defended, or retitle the video to the three episodes you really cover. Also say that the 'fourteen' is Sayer's count and that Spanish authors count differently.

Fix the balance with the same tools you already use: give the Spanish legal points (Utrecht Article X first-refusal clause, the Spanish exile at San Roque, the 1969 reasons and the UN decolonisation line) as much space as the British points, and add the missing Spanish and French names and human detail in the Great Siege (Córdova, Barceló, the camps). On every casualty number, say in one clause who counted and when, and explain the gap between 185, 357 and 2,000+ instead of putting the cards side by side.

Simplify what is heard: cut the Ince tunnelling and the tunnel tour or move them to on-screen text, say each key date once in spoken form with the old-calendar note on screen only, never use two 'Charles the Third/III' without a clear tag (the Habsburg claimant vs Charles III of Spain), and limit each sentence to one number. Tighten the neutral-ground century with one concrete event so that the middle does not sag.
_prompt:
You are a Spanish history teacher from Algeciras who reads English well. You know the Gibraltar story from Spanish sources and you notice when an English-language video tilts toward the British side, uses loaded words, or counts casualties without saying who counted.

Below is the complete narration script of a documentary YouTube video titled "Why Gibraltar Was Besieged 14 Times" (about 11 minutes, English narration, animated maps and 3D reconstructions). Lines in [On screen: ...] are text shown on screen at that moment; [silent shot] means picture and music only. Read all of it as yourself and answer honestly. Do not be polite; you have no stake in who made it.

Check especially: (a) factual claims that seem wrong, overstated or missing a source; (b) sentences that favour one side (British or Spanish) by wording, emphasis or omission; (c) any casualty or loss number that does not say who counted it; (d) sentences that are hard to understand when heard once; (e) stretches where you would get bored or leave.

Return ONLY this JSON (no other text). In every "quote", copy the exact words from the script (a short exact phrase is fine):
{"main_message": "<one sentence>",
 "would_keep_watching_after_30s": true|false, "hook_1to10": n, "trust_1to10": n, "balance_1to10": n, "overall_1to10": n,
 "claims_doubted": [{"chapter": "<chapter title>", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "one_sided": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "favours": "British|Spanish", "why": "..."}],
 "casualty_counter_missing": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "hard_to_follow": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "boring_or_slow": [{"chapter": "...", "from_quote": "...", "why": "..."}],

=== SCRIPT ===
## Midnight at the Gate
Midnight at the Gibraltar frontier. To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
The Rock sits at the western gate of the Mediterranean.
Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
This is why everyone fought over it, told from both sides' records.
[On screen: "A history explainer · every date sourced · British and Spanish records side by side · Facts as of 18 Oct 2026"]
[On screen: number card "14 sieges · 1309–1783" — "Sayer 1862 · García Sanz 2022 · Gibraltar National Museum"]
In 1782, ten floating batteries came to break it.
In 1941, a runway was laid across the only road to Spain.
So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?

## 1704: A Rock Changes Hands
Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
That summer, their fleet sailed into the Bay of Gibraltar.
Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of the rival claimant, "Charles the Third."
This plan, printed in 1705, shows the prize: a walled town that historians on both sides would call the key of the Mediterranean.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «la preciosa llave del Mediterráneo» — "the precious key of the Mediterranean" · Sayer, 1862: "the key of the Mediterranean"]
Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender. The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «con cien hombres de guarnición … no había artilleros que las sirvieran» — "a garrison of a hundred men … there were no gunners to serve them"]
On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered.
[On screen: "4 August 1704 · English histories: 24 July 1704 (old calendar)"]
British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third." By Spanish accounts, almost all left, and the largest group settled a league north-east, at San Roque.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se habia acampado en las haciendas cercanas á la ermita de San Roque» — "had camped on the farms near the hermitage of San Roque"]
In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht made it permanent: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever." But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain said in 2015 that it does.
Spain besieged it twice more: from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and in 1727. Neither siege took it.
So in 1730, Philip the Fifth ordered a stone line across the isthmus, out of gun range, to cut Gibraltar off by land. The town behind it is still called La Línea: "the line."
[On screen: Gómez Nadal (Almoraima), on Philip V's order of 8 Oct 1730: «bloquear definitivamente la correspondencia y paso a la plaza por tierra» — "to block, once and for all, all contact with and passage to the town by land"]

## The Great Siege
Half a century later came a different question: can you starve a rock? On the twenty-first of June 1779, Madrid cut Gibraltar off from Spain.
Spain had joined France in its war with Britain. By October, by the British count, about fourteen thousand Spanish troops faced the Rock.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Carlos III declaró la guerra á Inglaterra y se unió á Francia» — "Charles III declared war on England and joined France"]
At sea, from mid-July, a Spanish squadron sealed the port. Based at Algeciras, its boats were there to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «encaminado principalmente á privar a la plaza de los viveres que le llegaban de las costas de África» — "aimed above all at depriving the town of the food that reached it from the coasts of Africa"]
By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many; an egg cost sixpence.
The governor, General Eliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea.
To break the blockade, Britain sent three relief fleets: 1780, 1781, 1782.
Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship of lemons was brought in, garrison diaries record.
On the twelfth of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor, and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town. The townspeople fled south.
Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
By British tallies, the two sides fired over four hundred and sixty thousand rounds.
By September 1782, the garrison counted about seven and a half thousand men.
The garrison turned to heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire. On the eighth of September, they used them in earnest against the Spanish works.
Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets gathered in the bay: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish. The Duc de Crillon led the siege.
[On screen: Fernández Duro, Armada española (1901): «alegrando la vista los 50 navios que se juntaron en Algeciras» — "the 50 ships of the line that gathered at Algeciras, a joy to see"]
Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
[On screen: Conseil de guerre privé (1785): «l'expérience que l'inventeur avoit demandée … à l'épreuve des boulets rouges» — "the test the inventor had asked for … against red-hot shot"]
The thirteenth of September 1782. That morning, the batteries moved into position, and the garrison opened fire on them. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, the attackers' guns, some four hundred, opened fire together. By the next afternoon, all ten batteries were lost.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «á las diez y veinte y cinco minutos de la mañana … rompieron á un tiempo el fuego» — "at twenty-five past ten in the morning … opened fire all at once"]
By British and Spanish counts, over two thousand attackers were lost, prisoners included; the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
[On screen: number card: "> 2,000 lost, prisoners included — British estimate & Montero (Spain)" · "185 hit by gunfire before the fires — French account, 1785" · "357 rescued — British return" · "Garrison: 16 killed — its own return" {S069} {S070} {S071}]
Before the attack, all summer, the garrison had been digging through the north face. By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
In July they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se formó un boquete tan grande … que pareció bien colocar en el un cañón» — "an opening was made so large … that it seemed right to place a cannon in it"]
The blockade never forced a surrender. In February 1783, word came of a preliminary peace, and on the fifth, the last shot was fired.
From all causes, the Spanish historian Montero put the losses near two thousand defenders and six thousand besiegers. The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and sixty-nine dead. Gibraltar stayed British.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Los últimos sufrieron una pérdida de cerca de dos mil hombres. La nuestra se aproximó á seis mil por todas causas» — "The latter [the besieged] suffered a loss of nearly two thousand men. Ours came close to six thousand, from all causes" · number card: "Garrison return (Drinkwater): 333 killed or died of wounds · 536 died of sickness (scurvy deaths 1779–80 not included)"]

## The Neutral Ground
Which leaves a question the treaty never answered: where does the Rock end? Between the walls and the Spanish line lay a strip of sand: the neutral ground.
In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
[On screen: Gómez de Avellaneda: «con autorización española, fueran destruidos por los ingleses» — "with Spanish authorisation, they were destroyed by the British" · "Montero gives 1811"]
After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «el progresivo avance de la frontera sobre la zona neutral» — "the gradual advance of the frontier over the neutral zone"]
On the Spanish side, a town grew up behind the old line. In 1870, it became La Línea de la Concepción.
Remember this street in La Línea. We'll come back to it.
This was the gap between them: a strip of neutral ground between two towns.
In 1908, Britain told Spain, "as an act of courtesy," that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground. The fence went up in 1909; Spain does not recognise it as a border.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «"como acto de cortesía"» — "as an act of courtesy"]
Behind the fence: a garrison camp, gardens, rifle ranges, a racecourse.
And from 1934, a grass airstrip was built there. Subscribe if you'd like the next place in this series.

## A Runway on the Isthmus
Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself. Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway; in 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain.
[On screen: Spanish government to its London ambassador, 4 Mar 1939 (Marquina Barrio, 1981): «una porción usurpada del territorio nacional» — "a usurped portion of the national territory"]
Then Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels.
Inside the Rock, those tunnels held a road about a mile long, a hospital and a power station, dug by British and Canadian tunnellers.
Gibraltar counts about fifty-five kilometres of tunnels from every era, more than its roads above ground.
This 1943 US Army map shows the town house by house, and the runway reaching into the bay.
June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier. Gibraltar sends its women and children away. By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.
[silent shot]
For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested what it called breaches of Spanish waters; no complaint over the airstrip is on record.
[On screen: Marquina Barrio, 1981: «no queda constancia de reclamaciones por el uso de la pista» — "there is no record of complaints over the use of the strip"]
On the night of the seventh of November 1942, by Gibraltar's official record, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway. The invasion fleets, from Britain and the United States, came through the Strait.

## The Gate
After the war, the argument returned to the gate. In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off. The gate fully reopened in 1985.
The same square, today. In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand. People on foot still cross the runway.
And on the other side of the gate.
Remember this street? In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
That spreads output over the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs. Our read: part of the work behind that number is done from the other side.
In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty; the next day, routine checks here ended.
It says it changes neither side's position on sovereignty. In July, Gibraltar's government said the old fence was coming down, with a new one a few metres behind; only about a hundred and fifty metres, where walkers cross, stays open.
As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is applied provisionally, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
So why did everyone fight over this place? Where it sits, and the sea that could feed it. A wall in 1704. A line in 1730. A fence in 1909. A runway in 1941.
[silent shot]
In 1730, Spain built a line to cut the Rock off by land. Today, four in ten of the Rock's jobs are held by people who live beyond it. The last siege ended in 1783. The argument didn't. Next in Contested Places: London, 1666.
